title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

paper.title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling.
Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training.
We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse.
Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades.
A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule.
Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a 16 × 16\times batch range support both predictions.
Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it.
Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain.
The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model.
Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure.
Our code is available at: two-clocks-rlvr .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: The two clocks under the square-root rule with μ = 8 \mu{=}8 . Color marks the rollout batch, from 512 in blue to 8,192 in dark red. Left, with the clip: samples to reach 15% and 20% accuracy, with the critical-batch curve (gray) between perfect invariance (dotted) and the step-limited extreme (dashed). Right: samples to failure without the clip, against the failure-law band (gray), with an open marker for the run that never failed. Progress slows with the batch, while failure stays on the failure law. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) has become a widely used post-training approach for language models, spanning mathematical reasoning ( Hubert et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , code ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025a ) , and broader domains scored against reference answers ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Its appeal is that large amounts of policy-generated data can be scored without human preference labels, but training remains expensive because this data must be regenerated as the policy changes: every policy update requires fresh rollouts, and generation dominates the cost. Practitioners therefore enlarge the rollout batch , the number of responses generated by one policy before it is updated, and rely on the square-root rule to transfer the learning rate across batch sizes, scaling it with the square root of the batch ( Malladi et al., 2022 ; Hilton et al., 2022 ) . For Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) with one optimizer step per rollout, the rule approximately works: rollout batches from 512 to 8K responses follow learning curves within about one accuracy point of each other when plotted against the number of samples consumed ( Li et al., 2026 ) . However, practical RLVR training rarely operates in this one-step regime. To amortize generation, practical RLVR recipes split each rollout into mini-batches and take one optimizer step on each. DAPO, for example, uses 16 optimizer steps per rollout ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . From the second step onward, the current policy has moved away from the policy that generated the data, so the token-level importance ratios depart from one and the PPO-style ratio clip begins to suppress gradient contributions from tokens whose ratios move beyond the clipping range. In our multi-step GRPO experiments, three phenomena appear together under the square-root rule: ➀ Progress slows with batch size. Larger rollout batches learn more slowly per sample. ➁ Failure keeps time in samples. Without the clip, larger batches collapse after the same number of samples as smaller ones, despite taking far fewer optimizer steps. ➂ Clipping helps larger batches most. Although clipping is often viewed as a bottleneck on learning ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , its stabilizing effect is strongest for the larger batches. Figure 1 visualizes this split into two clocks: progress becomes increasingly sample-inefficient with larger rollout batches, while failure stays locked to the number of samples consumed. Prior work studies these effects separately: batch-size invariance ( Hilton et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , critical-batch behavior with the learning rate tuned at every batch ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , and clipping at a fixed batch size. None explains why all three emerge together under the same batch-dependent learning-rate rule. We explain these phenomena with a two-clock framework of batch scaling. Its central observation is that the square-root rule preserves the policy’s drift per sample, the persistent displacement it accumulates, but not the progress that drift produces. A larger rollout batch takes fewer optimizer steps on the same samples, and the square-root rule makes each step longer. Under a local quadratic model, these fewer, longer steps accumulate the same drift per sample but lose more progress to curvature. This gives a progress clock , which counts samples to a target accuracy and slows beyond a learning-rate-dependent critical batch. If collapse occurs when accumulated drift reaches a threshold, the same scaling rule gives a failure clock that is invariant in samples. The progress clock follows from the local quadratic model, and the failure clock rests on a drift-threshold hypothesis that we test. We test the two-clock model with controlled GRPO experiments that vary rollout batch size, learning rate, and clipping over a sixteenfold range of rollout batches. The progress clock departs from sample invariance beyond a critical batch: with eight steps per rollout, as the learning rate rises tenfold, the sample-cost exponent climbs from 0.15 to 0.44. Unlike the tuned-learning-rate picture ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , the critical batch therefore shrinks with the learning rate assigned by the square-root rule and lies well below the gradient noise scale. The failure clock, in contrast, does not move along the rule: without the clip, a 4,096 batch fails after 56 to 80 optimizer steps and a 512 batch after 648, yet both fail after 30 to 50k samples. Restoring the clip delays collapse twofold for the small batch and fourfold for the large one, and the progress gap is present with or without it. The progress gap reappears on a second dataset, a second checkpoint, and a 7B model. The separation between the two clocks further yields a simple batch schedule: start below the critical batch for sample-efficient progress, then switch to a larger batch when throughput or stability makes it preferable. The ramp approaches the best fixed batch while generating three quarters of its samples at the large batch. To summarize, our contributions are as follows. ➀ We introduce a two-clock framework for multi-step GRPO, in which a local model derives a learning-rate-dependent critical batch for progress, while a drift-threshold hypothesis predicts failure at a fixed number of samples along the square-root rule. ➁ We test these predictions across batch size, learning rate, clipping, model scale, and dataset, with failure-law fits that favor drift scaling over noise-driven alternatives and clip and replay controls showing that the clip delays failure while the progress gap persists without it. ➂ We derive a practical batch schedule for multi-step RLVR from the two clocks: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. In our experiments, this schedule approaches the best fixed-batch performance.

sections.heading: 3 Method: A Two-Clock Model of Batch Scaling
sections.text: Figure 2: Schematic of the two-clock model, with small (blue) and large (red) batches at the same first-order drift per sample. (A) The large batch covers this drift in fewer, longer steps that lose more progress to curvature, so it needs more samples to reach the target τ \tau . (B) Token log-ratios spread with each step, about 8 \sqrt{8} times faster for the large batch, and the clip cuts tokens outside the band. sections.heading: Predictions.
sections.text: The model gives three testable predictions, corresponding to the three phenomena of the introduction. P1. Progress slows beyond a critical batch. Sample efficiency degrades with the batch as the curvature term becomes important, more so at higher learning rates, and even where the clip cannot act. P2. Failure keeps time in samples. Without the clip, the square-root rule preserves the failure point in samples, and lowering the learning rate delays failure linearly, as the drift law predicts, not quadratically, as a noise-driven 1 / η 2 1/\eta^{2} law would. P3. The clip buys stability rather than sustained speed. Larger batches are clipped more, so the clip should delay their failure most without removing the progress gap, and widening it should give this protection up.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We train Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B ( Yang et al., 2024 ) with GRPO in verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) on DAPO-Math-17k ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , using G = 8 G{=}8 , temperature 1, and responses up to 3072 tokens. We use AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) with a short linear warm-up followed by a constant learning rate. To isolate batch-size, learning-rate, and clipping effects, we disable KL penalty, entropy bonus, dynamic sampling, and gradient-norm clipping, and test gradient-norm clipping separately. Each run has a budget of 98,304 responses. We evaluate every 8,192 responses on 512 held-out problems, averaging four samples per problem. Additional details are in App. B .

sections.heading: Batches and learning rates.
sections.text: We use rollout batches of 512, 1536, 4096, and 8192 responses (S, M, L, and XL in Table 1 ), spanning a 16 × 16\times range. Unless stated otherwise, each rollout is split into μ = 8 \mu{=}8 optimizer steps. Learning rates follow the square-root rule from η S ∈ { 10 − 6 , 5 × 10 − 6 , 10 − 5 } \eta_{S}\in\{10^{-6},5{\times}10^{-6},10^{-5}\} . At 10 − 6 10^{-6} , clipping is almost never active, and we call this regime conservative . At the two larger rates, clipping becomes regularly active, and we call these regimes active .

sections.heading: Failure criterion.
sections.text: A run fails at the first point at which its accuracy falls below half of the best accuracy observed so far. If this never happens, we use the first sustained gradient-norm excursion: the first rollout whose gradient norm exceeds four times its early median and is followed by at least three of the next eight rollouts above the same threshold. Runs meeting neither condition within the training budget are right-censored.

sections.heading: The failure pattern favors accumulated drift.
sections.text: Failure depends on the learning rate far more weakly than the quadratic law of a noise-driven random walk, and at the highest learning rates it coincides with a jump of about four orders of magnitude in the KL divergence between the updated and rollout policies. The failure point is also not an artifact of disabling gradient-norm clipping: with a norm cap of 1.0, the small batch fails after 36k samples, within the 31–46k range of its seeds.

sections.heading: Robustness.
sections.text: Failure also keeps time in samples on the 7B model, with a model-specific constant. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, the two batches fail 6 × 6\times apart in rollouts but only 1.3 × 1.3\times apart in samples. Along the square-root rule, larger batches thus fail after the same number of consumed samples despite taking far fewer optimizer steps.

sections.heading: 5.3 The clip buys stability rather than sustained speed (P3)

sections.heading: The clip delays failure, most for the large batch.
sections.text: With the clip on, the small batch still fails, but later, by a factor of two (Fig. 6 ). The large batch, which clips several times more tokens per step, never fails within our training budget at its scaled rates. Pushed to twice its rate so that it does fail, it lasts four times longer with the clip than without, while the small batch with a similar unclipped failure point gains only a factor of two. As the model predicts, the stabilizing effect is largest for the batch on which clipping acts most strongly. A practical side effect: since clipped runs always outlive the unclipped law, Eq. ( 7 ) is a conservative estimate of when a clipped run can fail.

sections.heading: What the clip removes.
sections.text: In replays of frozen checkpoints, only about 0.5% of the large batch’s tokens are clipped, yet their gradient has more than half the norm of the full gradient, while the share is much smaller for the small batch (App. A.4 , App. E.1 ). Clipping therefore removes a large, batch-dependent part of the update, as the wider ratio spread of the large batch predicts.

sections.heading: Widening the clip trades stability for a transient gain.
sections.text: Widening the clip reduces the clipped fraction and speeds early learning, but the gain is not sustained: performance later decays and one of two seeds collapses (App. E.2 ). Allowing ratios to move farther therefore gives up much of the large batch’s stability without recovering sustained sample efficiency. Overall, the clip trades a transient speed-up for stability, a trade that favors large batches.

sections.heading: 6 Implications
sections.text: Figure 7: Batch ramp with η S = 5 × 10 − 6 \eta_{S}{=}5{\times}10^{-6} and μ = 8 \mu{=}8 . Each ramp uses batch 512 for 24.6k samples (dotted line), then switches to 4,096 or 8,192 (two seeds each), and thin lines are fixed batches. Both ramps lie well above the fixed large batches, near the best fixed batch. The two clocks give a simple batch-selection rule. Its one free choice, the switch point, is forgiving over a broad range.

sections.heading: Below the critical batch, use the largest efficient batch.
sections.text: Since progress changes little below B ∗ B^{*} while larger batches are no less stable, the model favors the largest batch that remains below the critical regime. At our learning rates this is 1,536 responses: it matches the small batch’s sample efficiency to within seed noise, does not fail, and achieves the best final accuracy among the fixed batches.

sections.heading: Above the critical batch, ramp the batch.
sections.text: When a larger batch is needed for throughput, train first with a small batch and switch, before its predicted failure point, to a larger and more stable batch. We reset the optimizer state and repeat the one-rollout warm-up at the switch. The resulting ramps lie well above the fixed large-batch curves and track the best fixed batch, while generating three quarters of their samples with the large batch (Fig. 7 ). App. G finds that switches between 25k and 74k samples perform similarly, and the failure law bounds how late the switch can come.

sections.heading: Batch-size scaling and invariance.
sections.text: Batch size is a basic scaling variable in optimization, affecting both computational efficiency and training dynamics. The linear rule for SGD ( Smith et al., 2018 ) , which also motivates growing the batch during training, and the square-root rule for Adam ( Malladi et al., 2022 ) keep training trajectories comparable across batch sizes. Hilton et al. (2022) make PPO batch-size invariant by decoupling the clip’s proximal policy from the behavior policy, given a sufficiently small optimizer batch, while Li et al. (2026) show that square-root scaling keeps GRPO learning curves aligned with one optimizer step per rollout over a bounded range of batch sizes. In contrast, we study the multi-step regime, where this batch-size invariance no longer holds and drift preservation does not imply progress preservation.

sections.heading: Critical batch.
sections.text: Beyond a critical batch, larger batches stop saving optimizer steps and start costing samples. With the learning rate re-tuned at every batch, the critical batch of McCandlish et al. (2018) equals the gradient noise scale and does not depend on the learning rate. Under square-root scaling, by contrast, the learning rate is coupled to batch size, leading to a different critical batch that depends on the learning-rate scale. In LLM RL, larger batches have been found to reach higher final accuracy ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Khatri et al., 2026 ) while learning more slowly ( Khatri et al., 2026 ) . Our two-clock view connects these observations by separating the batch scale governing progress from the sample scale governing failure.

sections.heading: Training collapse.
sections.text: Batch scaling also affects training stability. Suk and Duan (2025) derive a step-size threshold above which RLVR collapses, while Song et al. (2026) find that collapse time in asynchronous GRPO scales roughly as 1 / η 1/\eta , the fixed-batch case of Eq. ( 7 ), and attribute it to directional drift. We add the batch dimension: along the square-root rule, failure is approximately invariant in consumed samples.

sections.heading: Ratio clipping.
sections.text: Training stability in GRPO is closely tied to ratio clipping. Trust-region methods replace or soften the hard clip ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Dwyer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Jia et al., 2026 ) , while Tian et al. (2026) relax it to enable stale-rollout reuse and Khatri et al. (2026) show that the clip threshold changes RL scaling behavior. In contrast to work that treats clipping as a bottleneck ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , we find that it mainly buys stability, at a transient cost in speed.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Scaling rules are often interpreted as promises of invariance. For multi-step GRPO, the square-root rule instead preserves first-order drift per sample, not progress per sample, yielding two clocks: progress slows beyond a learning-rate-dependent critical batch, while a drift-threshold hypothesis predicts an approximately sample-invariant failure point. Our experiments support these predictions and show that ratio clipping buys stability, especially for larger batches, while the progress gap persists without it. Together, the two clocks suggest a simple strategy for multi-step RLVR: train below the critical batch for efficient progress, then switch to a larger batch before failure when throughput demands it.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We broaden our evaluation across multiple checkpoints, two datasets, and a 7B model, but compute and resource constraints still limit our coverage to one model family and one task domain. Our theory is intentionally local, and direct measurement of the curvature term is computationally expensive at this scale, so we evaluate it through its testable predictions. Failure points also exhibit intrinsic variation across seeds. Finally, we measure sample efficiency in responses, while token, compute, and wall-clock efficiency additionally depend on generation lengths, hardware, and system implementation.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This work analyzes the training dynamics of RLVR on public math datasets with open-weight models and releases no new model or dataset. Its main societal relevance is environmental: our batch schedule aims to reduce the number of generated samples a large batch needs to reach a given accuracy, although our own study required many training runs (App. B reports the hardware). We see no additional risks beyond those of LLM post-training in general.

sections.heading: On (A3).
sections.text: The threshold assumption is the model’s one empirical hypothesis, and the failure-law fit of § 5.2 tests the exponents it predicts. The threshold concerns movement along the slowly varying mean-gradient direction, where drift accumulates linearly in the samples consumed, whereas noise, spread over many directions, contributes only a random-walk component. It predicts γ = 1 \gamma=1 and β = 1 2 \beta=\tfrac{1}{2} , the noise-driven alternative γ = 2 \gamma=2 and β = 1 \beta=1 , and a batch-blind drift γ = 1 \gamma=1 and β = 0 \beta=0 . The fit excludes the second, since Table 4 gives γ ≈ 0.7 \gamma\approx 0.7 , and pins the combination β − γ / 2 \beta-\gamma/2 that the scaling rule probes near zero, which (A3) predicts and the third alternative does not.

sections.heading: Clip-active steps.
sections.text: For the same N N samples a run takes N / b N/b optimizer steps, of which the fraction ( μ − 1 ) / μ (\mu-1)/\mu with k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 can clip: 1344 for S against 168 for L at 98k. If failure required accumulating some number of clip-active steps, the small batch would reach it after eight times fewer samples. The unclipped runs rule this out: at the gradient-norm onset, L fails after 7 rollouts, or 56 optimizer steps (29k samples), and S after 81 rollouts, or 648 optimizer steps (41k), a 1.4 × 1.4\times difference in samples against 12 × 12\times in steps. sections.heading: Budgets.
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, runs consume 98,304 responses, and selected failure probes use longer budgets.

sections.heading: Choosing the learning rates.
sections.text: We first ran 24-rollout probes of the small batch over η ∈ { 10 − 6 , 5 × 10 − 6 , 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 } \eta\in\{10^{-6},5{\times}10^{-6},10^{-5},2{\times}10^{-5}\} . Clipping was essentially inactive at 10 − 6 10^{-6} , became regularly active at 5 × 10 − 6 5{\times}10^{-6} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and was stronger at 2 × 10 − 5 2{\times}10^{-5} . We therefore use 10 − 6 10^{-6} as the conservative rate and the next two as the active rates. Separate ladders are used for μ = 1 \mu{=}1 , Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-Math-7B, and App. F describes the Instruct ladder.

sections.heading: Exact ratios at the first step.
sections.text: Dynamic token packing makes the rollout and the recomputed log-probabilities use differently shaped micro-batches, and under bf16 this produces spurious deviations from ρ = 1 \rho=1 at k = 0 k{=}0 , with the 99th percentile of | log ⁡ ρ | |\log\rho| reaching 0.03–0.12. Fixed micro-batches of four sequences in identical order make the ratio exactly one. All runs use this setting except the seed-0 small-batch runs in the conservative regime, where this noise stays inside the clip range: no token is clipped at k = 0 k{=}0 in that regime, as App. C confirms.

sections.heading: Hardware and compute.
sections.text: The 1.5B experiments used four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs per run, while the 7B experiments used four H100 GPUs. In total, the experiments used roughly 2,000 GPU-hours, including preliminary runs and the replay analyses.

Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Junwei Quan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Toronto yuantel@cs.cmu.edu, junwei.quan@mail.utoronto.ca Kai Qiu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Kate Zhang Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Yicheng Tao Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a 16 × 16	imes batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: two-clocks-rlvr . 1 Introduction Figure 1: The two clocks under the square-root rule with μ = 8 \mu{=}8 . Color marks the rollout batch, from 512 in blue to 8,192 in dark red. Left, with the clip: samples to reach 15% and 20% accuracy, with the critical-batch curve (gray) between perfect invariance (dotted) and the step-limited extreme (dashed). Right: samples to failure without the clip, against the failure-law band (gray), with an open marker for the run that never failed. Progress slows with the batch, while failure stays on the failure law. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) has become a widely used post-training approach for language models, spanning mathematical reasoning ( Hubert et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) , code ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025a ) , and broader domains scored against reference answers ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Its appeal is that large amounts of policy-generated data can be scored without human preference labels, but training remains expensive because this data must be regenerated as the policy changes: every policy update requires fresh rollouts, and generation dominates the cost. Practitioners therefore enlarge the rollout batch , the number of responses generated by one policy before it is updated, and rely on the square-root rule to transfer the learning rate across batch sizes, scaling it with the square root of the batch ( Malladi et al., 2022 ; Hilton et al., 2022 ) . For Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) with one optimizer step per rollout, the rule approximately works: rollout batches from 512 to 8K responses follow learning curves within about one accuracy point of each other when plotted against the number of samples consumed ( Li et al., 2026 ) . However, practical RLVR training rarely operates in this one-step regime. To amortize generation, practical RLVR recipes split each rollout into mini-batches and take one optimizer step on each. DAPO, for example, uses 16 optimizer steps per rollout ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . From the second step onward, the current policy has moved away from the policy that generated the data, so the token-level importance ratios depart from one and the PPO-style ratio clip begins to suppress gradient contributions from tokens whose ratios move beyond the clipping range. In our multi-step GRPO experiments, three phenomena appear together under the square-root rule: ➀ Progress slows with batch size. Larger rollout batches learn more slowly per sample. ➁ Failure keeps time in samples. Without the clip, larger batches collapse after the same number of samples as smaller ones, despite taking far fewer optimizer steps. ➂ Clipping helps larger batches most. Although clipping is often viewed as a bottleneck on learning ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , its stabilizing effect is strongest for the larger batches. Figure 1 visualizes this split into two clocks: progress becomes increasingly sample-inefficient with larger rollout batches, while failure stays locked to the number of samples consumed. Prior work studies these effects separately: batch-size invariance ( Hilton et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , critical-batch behavior with the learning rate tuned at every batch ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , and clipping at a fixed batch size. None explains why all three emerge together under the same batch-dependent learning-rate rule. We explain these phenomena with a two-clock framework of batch scaling. Its central observation is that the square-root rule preserves the policy’s drift per sample, the persistent displacement it accumulates, but not the progress that drift produces. A larger rollout batch takes fewer optimizer steps on the same samples, and the square-root rule makes each step longer. Under a local quadratic model, these fewer, longer steps accumulate the same drift per sample but lose more progress to curvature. This gives a progress clock , which counts samples to a target accuracy and slows beyond a learning-rate-dependent critical batch. If collapse occurs when accumulated drift reaches a threshold, the same scaling rule gives a failure clock that is invariant in samples. The progress clock follows from the local quadratic model, and the failure clock rests on a drift-threshold hypothesis that we test. We test the two-clock model with controlled GRPO experiments that vary rollout batch size, learning rate, and clipping over a sixteenfold range of rollout batches. The progress clock departs from sample invariance beyond a critical batch: with eight steps per rollout, as the learning rate rises tenfold, the sample-cost exponent climbs from 0.15 to 0.44. Unlike the tuned-learning-rate picture ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , the critical batch therefore shrinks with the learning rate assigned by the square-root rule and lies well below the gradient noise scale. The failure clock, in contrast, does not move along the rule: without the clip, a 4,096 batch fails after 56 to 80 optimizer steps and a 512 batch after 648, yet both fail after 30 to 50k samples. Restoring the clip delays collapse twofold for the small batch and fourfold for the large one, and the progress gap is present with or without it. The progress gap reappears on a second dataset, a second checkpoint, and a 7B model. The separation between the two clocks further yields a simple batch schedule: start below the critical batch for sample-efficient progress, then switch to a larger batch when throughput or stability makes it preferable. The ramp approaches the best fixed batch while generating three quarters of its samples at the large batch. To summarize, our contributions are as follows. ➀ We introduce a two-clock framework for multi-step GRPO, in which a local model derives a learning-rate-dependent critical batch for progress, while a drift-threshold hypothesis predicts failure at a fixed number of samples along the square-root rule. ➁ We test these predictions across batch size, learning rate, clipping, model scale, and dataset, with failure-law fits that favor drift scaling over noise-driven alternatives and clip and replay controls showing that the clip delays failure while the progress gap persists without it. ➂ We derive a practical batch schedule for multi-step RLVR from the two clocks: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Batch size is a basic scaling variable in optimization, affecting both computational efficiency and training dynamics. The linear rule for SGD ( Smith et al., 2018 ) , which also motivates growing the batch during training, and the square-root rule for Adam ( Malladi et al., 2022 ) keep training trajectories comparable across batch sizes. Hilton et al. (2022) make PPO batch-size invariant by decoupling the clip’s proximal policy from the behavior policy, given a sufficiently small optimizer batch, while Li et al. (2026) show that square-root scaling keeps GRPO learning curves aligned with one optimizer step per rollout over a bounded range of batch sizes. In contrast, we study the multi-step regime, where this batch-size invariance no longer holds and drift preservation does not imply progress preservation. Critical batch. Beyond a critical batch, larger batches stop saving optimizer steps and start costing samples. With the learning rate re-tuned at every batch, the critical batch of McCandlish et al. (2018) equals the gradient noise scale and does not depend on the learning rate. Under square-root scaling, by contrast, the learning rate is coupled to batch size, leading to a different critical batch that depends on the learning-rate scale. In LLM RL, larger batches have been found to reach higher final accuracy ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Khatri et al., 2026 ) while learning more slowly ( Khatri et al., 2026 ) . Our two-clock view connects these observations by separating the batch scale governing progress from the sample scale governing failure. Training collapse. Batch scaling also affects training stability. Suk and Duan (2025) derive a step-size threshold above which RLVR collapses, while Song et al. (2026) find that collapse time in asynchronous GRPO scales roughly as 1 / η 1/\eta , the fixed-batch case of Eq. ( 7 ), and attribute it to directional drift. We add the batch dimension: along the square-root rule, failure is approximately invariant in consumed samples. Ratio clipping. Training stability in GRPO is closely tied to ratio clipping. Trust-region methods replace or soften the hard clip ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Dwyer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Jia et al., 2026 ) , while Tian et al. (2026) relax it to enable stale-rollout reuse and Khatri et al. (2026) show that the clip threshold changes RL scaling behavior. In contrast to work that treats clipping as a bottleneck ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , we find that it mainly buys stability, at a transient cost in speed. 8 Conclusion Scaling rules are often interpreted as promises of invariance. For multi-step GRPO, the square-root rule instead preserves first-order drift per sample, not progress per sample, yielding two clocks: progress slows beyond a learning-rate-dependent critical batch, while a drift-threshold hypothesis predicts an approximately sample-invariant failure point. Our experiments support these predictions and show that ratio clipping buys stability, especially for larger batches, while the progress gap persists without it. Together, the two clocks suggest a simple strategy for multi-step RLVR: train below the critical batch for efficient progress, then switch to a larger batch before failure when throughput demands it. Limitations We broaden our evaluation across multiple checkpoints, two datasets, and a 7B model, but compute and resource constraints still limit our coverage to one model family and one task domain. Our theory is intentionally local, and direct measurement of the curvature term is computationally expensive at this scale, so we evaluate it through its testable predictions. Failure points also exhibit intrinsic variation across seeds. Finally, we measure sample efficiency in responses, while token, compute, and wall-clock efficiency additionally depend on generation lengths, hardware, and system implementation. Ethical Considerations This work analyzes the training dynamics of RLVR on public math datasets with open-weight models and releases no new model or dataset. Its main societal relevance is environmental: our batch schedule aims to reduce the number of generated samples a large batch needs to reach a given accuracy, although our own study required many training runs (App. B reports the hardware). We see no additional risks beyond those of LLM post-training in general. References Dwyer et al. (2025) M. Dwyer, A. Sobey, and A.
